Definition / Description: The interest rate the Bank of England pays on overnight reserves held by commercial banks; it is the primary lever for influencing economy‑wide borrowing and saving rates.

Term: Bank of England Asset Purchase Facility Fund Limited (BEAPFF)
Definition / Description: A wholly‑owned Bank of England company that conducts asset purchases (UK government and selected corporate bonds) on behalf of the Monetary Policy Committee.
A fixed‑income IOU issued by governments or companies that pays a stated annual **coupon** and returns principal at maturity; its price and **yield** move inversely.
Digital money the Bank of England creates and credits to banks’ reserve accounts; used to settle payments and to finance bond purchases under quantitative easing.
The inflation measure targeted by the Bank of England; calculated by the Office for National Statistics from a representative basket of around 700 goods and services.
A bond issued by a private‑sector company; the Bank purchased £20 billion of these under its quantitative‑easing programme to lower corporate borrowing costs.
The fixed cash interest payment on a bond (e.g. £5 per £100 of face value each year).
The annual percentage rise in the general level of prices for goods and services; the Bank aims to keep CPI inflation at 2 %.
The percentage cost of borrowing or return on saving per year; influenced across the economy by changes in Bank Rate and long‑term yields.

Large‑scale purchases of bonds financed with newly created central‑bank reserves, designed to raise bond prices, lower long‑term interest rates, and stimulate spending when Bank Rate is near its lower bound.
The reduction of the stock of bonds acquired under QE, achieved by allowing maturities to run off and/or actively selling holdings; restores capacity to deploy QE again if needed.
The bond’s annual return expressed as its coupon divided by current market price; as price rises, yield falls (e.g. a £5 coupon on a £120 price equals a 4.2 % yield).
The relationship across maturities of government‑bond yields; QE aims to flatten the longer‑maturity portion to ease economy‑wide borrowing costs.
